{{Short description|Bet sizing formula for long-term growth}}
[[File:Kelly bet.png|thumb|Example of the optimal Kelly betting fraction, versus expected return of other fractional bets.]]

In [[finance]], the '''Kelly criterion''' (or '''Kelly strategy''' or '''Kelly bet''') is a [[formula]] for risk allocation with the sizing a sequence of bets by maximizing the long-term [[expected value]] of the logarithm of wealth, which is equivalent to maximizing the long-term expected [[Geometric mean|geometric growth rate]].  [[John Larry Kelly Jr.]], a researcher at [[Bell Labs]], described the criterion in 1956.<ref name="original Kelly article">{{Cite journal |last=Kelly |first=J. L. |author-link=John Larry Kelly Jr. |date=1956 |title=A New Interpretation of Information Rate |url=https://www.princeton.edu/~wbialek/rome/refs/kelly_56.pdf |journal=[[Bell System Technical Journal]] |volume=35 |issue=4 |pages=917–926 |doi=10.1002/j.1538-7305.1956.tb03809.x }}</ref>

The practical use of the formula has been demonstrated for [[gambling]],<ref>{{cite conference |last=Thorp |first=E. O. |title=Fortune's Formula: The Game of Blackjack |date=January 1961 |conference=American Mathematical Society }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Thorp |first=Edward O. |title=Beat the Dealer: A Winning Strategy for the Game of Twenty-One: A Scientific Analysis of the World-Wide Game Known Variously as Blackjack, Twenty-One, Vingt-et-Un, Pontoon, or Van-John |publisher=Random House |publication-place=New York |date=1966 |isbn=0-394-70310-3 |oclc=655875 }}</ref> and the same idea was used to explain [[Diversification (finance)|diversification]] in [[investment management]].<ref name="Beat the Market">{{cite book |last1=Thorp |first1=Edward O. |last2=Kassouf |first2=Sheen T. |date=1967 |title=Beat the Market: A Scientific Stock Market System |url=http://www.edwardothorp.com/sitebuildercontent/sitebuilderfiles/beatthemarket.pdf |archive-url=https://www.economics.uci.edu/files/kassouf/pdfs/beatthemarket.pdf |publisher=Random House |isbn=0-394-42439-5 |archive-date=2009-10-07 |url-status=dead }}, page 184f.</ref> In the 2000s, Kelly-style analysis became a part of mainstream investment theory and the claim has been made that well-known, successful investors including [[Warren Buffett]] and [[William H. Gross|Bill Gross]] use Kelly methods (also see [[intertemporal portfolio choice]]).<ref>{{Citation |last=Pabrai |first=Mohnish |title=The Dhandho Investor: The Low-Risk Value Method to High Returns |url=https://archive.org/details/dhandhoinvestorl00pabr_0 |date=2007 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0-470-04389-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last=Thorp |first=E. O. |title=The Kelly Criterion: Part II |date=September 2008 |work=[[Wilmott (magazine)|Wilmott]] |page= }}</ref>{{Page needed|date=March 2026}}<ref>{{Citation |last1=Zenios |first1=S. A. |last2=Ziemba |first2=W. T. |date=2006 |title=Handbook of Asset and Liability Management |publisher=North Holland |isbn=978-0-444-50875-1 }}</ref><ref name="Poundstone book article">{{cite book |last=Poundstone |first=William |title=Fortune's Formula: The Untold Story of the Scientific Betting System That Beat the Casinos and Wall Street |url=https://archive.org/details/fortunesformulau00poun |date=2005 |place=New York |publisher=Hill and Wang |isbn=0-8090-4637-7 }}</ref> It is also the standard replacement of [[Power of a test|statistical power]] in anytime-valid statistical tests and confidence intervals, based on [[E-values|e-values and e-processes]].

==Relative bet sizes==
Gamblers often state the size of their bets relative to the Kelly criterion. A '''full Kelly''' bet is a bet made at the Kelly Criterion. A '''half Kelly''' bet is half the size of a full Kelly bet. A '''quarter Kelly''' bet is a quarter of the size of a full Kelly. Gamblers would use less than full Kelly in order to reduce the chance of ruin, reduce volatility, and account for model error. Due to the high drawdowns, gamblers in practice find fractional Kellies much better emotionally than full Kelly. This reduced volatility is a tradeoff, as it increases the time to reach an intended wealth or decreases the wealth growth rate. It has been found that betting an amount larger than the Kelly amount increases the [[risk of ruin]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=MacLean |first1=Leonard |last2=Thorp |first2=Edward |last3=Ziemba |first3=William |date=January 1, 2010 |title=Good and bad properties of the Kelly criterion |url=https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/157/Papers/Good_Bad_Kelly.pdf |publisher=self-published |access-date=2026-03-04 }}</ref>

== Binary return rates ==
In a system where the return on an investment or a bet is binary, so an interested party either wins or loses a fixed percentage of their bet, the expected growth rate coefficient yields a very specific solution for an optimal betting percentage.

=== Formula ===
The Kelly bet is:<ref name="edwardothorp.com">{{Cite web |last=Thorp |first=Edward O. |date=June 1997 |title=The Kelly criterion in blackjack, sports betting, and the stock market |url=https://www.eecs.harvard.edu/cs286r/courses/fall12/papers/Thorpe_KellyCriterion2007.pdf |access-date=2024-03-20 |website=10th International Conference on Gambling and Risk Taking |place=Montreal}}</ref>{{rp|7}}
<math display="block">f = \frac{p}{l}-\frac{q}{g}</math>
where:
* <math>f</math> is the fraction of the assets to apply to the security.
* <math>p</math> is the probability that the investment increases in value.
* <math>q</math> is the probability that the investment decreases in value (<math>q = 1 - p</math>).
* <math>g</math> is the fraction that is gained in a positive outcome.<ref name="edwardothorp.com" />{{rp|7}}  If the security price rises 10%, then <math>g = 0.1</math>.
* <math>l</math> is the fraction that is lost in a negative outcome.<ref name="edwardothorp.com" />{{rp|7}}  If the security price falls 10%, then <math>l = 0.1</math>.  In gambling, typically the entire wager is lost, which corresponds to {{tmath|1=l=1.0}}.
Note that the Kelly criterion is perfectly valid only for ''fully known'' outcome probabilities, which is almost never the case with investments. In addition, [[Risk aversion|risk-averse]] strategies invest less than the full Kelly fraction.

The general form can be rewritten as follows 
<math display="block">f = \frac{p}{l} \left( 1 -\frac{1-p}{p} \frac{l}{g} \right) = \frac{p}{l} \left( 1 -\frac{1}{\mathit{PR}} \frac{1}{\mathit{RRR}} \right)</math>
where:
* <math>\mathit{PR}=\frac{p}{1-p}</math> is the win-loss probability ratio, which is the ratio of probabilities of winning to losing bets.
* <math>\mathit{RRR}=\frac{g}{l}</math> is the reward-to-risk ratio of outcome sizes, which is the ''winning skew''.
It is clear that, at least, one of the factors <math>\mathit{PR}</math> or <math>\mathit{RRR}</math> needs to be larger than 1 for having an edge (so <math>f > 0</math>). It is even possible that the win-loss probability ratio is unfavorable <math>\mathit{PR} < 1</math>, but one has an edge as long as <math>\mathit{PR} \times \mathit{RRR} > 1</math>.

The Kelly formula can easily result in a fraction higher than 1, such as with losing size <math>l \ll 1</math> (see the above expression with factors of <math>\mathit{RRR}</math> and <math>\mathit{PR}</math>). This happens somewhat counterintuitively, because the Kelly fraction formula compensates for a small losing size with a larger bet. However, in most real situations, there is high uncertainty about all parameters entering the Kelly formula. In the case of a Kelly fraction higher than 1, it is theoretically advantageous to use [[Leverage (finance)|leverage]] to purchase additional securities on [[margin (finance)|margin]].

=== Example ===
In a study, each participant was given $25 and asked to place [[Even money|even-money bets]] on a coin that would land heads 60% of the time. Participants had 30 minutes to play, so could place about 300 bets, and the prizes were capped at $250.  But the behavior of the test subjects was far from optimal:
{{blockquote|Remarkably, 28% of the participants went bust, and the average payout was just $91. Only 21% of the participants reached the maximum. 18 of the 61 participants bet everything on one toss, while two-thirds gambled on tails at some stage in the experiment.<ref>{{Cite SSRN |title=Rational Decision-Making under Uncertainty: Observed Betting Patterns on a Biased Coin |last=Haghani |first=Victor |last2=Dewey |first2=Richard |date=19 October 2016 |ssrn=2856963}} {{arxiv|1701.01427}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Buttonwood |url=https://www.economist.com/blogs/buttonwood/2016/11/investing |title=Irrational tossers |work=[[The Economist]] |date=1 November 2016 }}</ref>}}

Using the Kelly criterion and based on the odds in the experiment (ignoring the cap of $250 and the finite duration of the test), the right approach would be to bet 20% of one's bankroll on each toss of the coin, which works out to a 2.034% average gain each round. This is a [[geometric mean]], not the arithmetic rate of 4% (r = 0.2 x (0.6 - 0.4) = 0.04).  The geometric mean wealth after 300 rounds works out to $10,505 (<math>= 25 \cdot (1.02034) ^ {300}</math>) if it were not capped.

In this particular game, because of the cap, a strategy of betting only 12% of the pot on each toss would have even better results (a 95% probability of reaching the cap and an average payout of $242.03).

=== Proof ===
Heuristic proofs of the Kelly criterion are straightforward.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Press |first1=W.H. |last2=Teukolsky |first2=S.A. |last3=Vetterling |first3=W.T. |last4=Flannery |first4=B.P. |date=2007 |title=Numerical Recipes: The Art of Scientific Computing |chapter=Section 14.7 (Example 2.) |chapter-url=https://faculty.kfupm.edu.sa/phys/aanaqvi/Numerical%20Recipes-The%20Art%20of%20Scientific%20Computing%203rd%20Edition%20(Press%20et%20al).pdf#page=782 |edition=3rd |place=New York |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-88068-8 }}</ref> The Kelly criterion maximizes the [[expected value]] of the logarithm of wealth (the expectation value of a function is given by the sum, over all possible outcomes, of the probability of each particular outcome multiplied by the value of the function in the event of that outcome). We start with 1 unit of wealth and bet a fraction <math>f</math> of that wealth. The probability of winning is <math>p</math>, the payoff multiplier is <math>g</math>, and the resulting wealth is equal to <math>1+fg</math>.  The probability of losing is <math>q=1-p</math>, the loss multiplier is <math>l</math>, and the resulting wealth is equal to <math>1-fl</math>. Therefore, we are trying to maximize the utility {{tmath|u}}:
<math display="block">u = p \log(1+fg)+q\log(1-fl) \,.</math>
To find the value of <math>f</math> for which the utility is maximized, we differentiate the above expression with respect to {{tmath|f}} and set this equal to zero. This gives:
<math display="block">0=\frac{du}{df}=\frac{pg}{1+fg}+\frac{-ql}{1-fl}\,.</math>
Rearranging this equation to solve for the value of <math>f</math> gives the Kelly criterion:
<math display="block">f = \frac{p}{l}-\frac{q}{g}\,.</math>
To be thorough, we should also consider the behaviour as <math>f</math> approaches the boundaries <math>-\frac{1}{g}</math> and <math>\frac{1}{l}</math> since there can be a maximum there without the derivative being 0. But <math>u</math> tends to −∞ for both. Finally, we need to show that the critical point found is not a minimum; this can be shown by computing the second derivative which is strictly negative for all <math>f</math> in the domain.

For this value of {{tmath|f}}, the wealth after a win would be {{tmath|1=1 + fg = 1 + \left(\frac{p}{l}-\frac{q}{g}\right) g = p\left(1 + \frac{g}{l}\right)}} and the wealth after a loss would be {{tmath|1=1 - fl = 1 - \left(\frac{p}{l}-\frac{q}{g}\right) l = q\left(1 + \frac{l}{g}\right)}}.

The expected geometric growth rate is {{tmath|1=r=\exp(u)}}, which is {{tmath|1=r=(1+fg)^p (1-fl)^q}}.

== Non-binary return rates ==
If the return rates on an investment or a bet are continuous in nature the optimal growth rate coefficient must take all possible events into account.

=== Application to the stock market ===
In [[mathematical finance]], if security weights maximize the expected geometric growth rate (which is equivalent to maximizing log wealth), then a portfolio is ''growth optimal.''

The Kelly Criterion shows that for a given volatile security this is satisfied when

<math>f = \frac {\mu - r} {\sigma^2}</math>

where <math>f</math> is the fraction of available capital invested that maximizes the expected geometric growth rate, <math>\mu</math> is the expected growth rate coefficient, <math>\sigma^2</math> is the [[variance]] of the growth rate coefficient and <math>r</math> is the risk-free rate of return. Note that a symmetric [[probability density function]] was assumed here.

Computations of growth optimal portfolios can suffer tremendous [[garbage in, garbage out]] problems. For example, the cases below take as given the [[expected return]] and covariance structure of assets, but these parameters are at best estimates or models that have significant uncertainty. If portfolio weights are largely a function of estimation errors, then ''Ex-post'' performance of a growth-optimal portfolio may differ fantastically from the ''ex-ante'' prediction. Parameter uncertainty and estimation errors are a large topic in portfolio theory. An approach to counteract the unknown risk is to invest less than the Kelly criterion.

Rough estimates are still useful. If we take excess return 6% and [[volatility (finance)|volatility]] 15% then the yearly [[Sharpe ratio]] is {{math|1=(''μ'' − ''r'')/''σ'' = 40%}}.  The Kelly fraction (i.e., the appropriate investment) for these values is {{math|1=(''μ'' − ''r'')/''σ''{{sup|2}} = 267%}}.  (That is, one could achieve the Kelly criterion by investing in a diverse set of stocks with a [[Beta (finance)|beta]] of 2.67.)  However the market invests 100% in itself so the market is apparently making its investment decisions using {{math|1=1 / 2.67 = 37.5%}} of the Kelly criterion value.

A detailed paper by [[Edward O. Thorp]] and a co-author estimates Kelly fraction to be 117% for the American stock market SP500 index.
<ref name="Thorp1992">{{Cite journal |last1=Thorp |first1=E. O. |last2=Rotando |first2=Louis M. |date=1992 |title=The Kelly criterion and the Stock Market |url=https://www.edwardothorp.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/TheKellyCriterionAndTheStockMarket.pdf |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=99 |issue=10 |pages=922–931 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1992.11995955}}</ref> Significant downside tail-risk for equity markets is another reason<ref name="Turlakov2017">{{Cite journal |last1=Turlakov |first1=Mihail |date=2017 |title=Leverage and Uncertainty |journal=Journal of Investment Strategies |pages=81–97 |volume=6 |arxiv=1612.07194 |doi=10.21314/JOIS.2017.087}}</ref> to reduce Kelly fraction from naive estimate (for instance, to reduce to half-Kelly).

== Proof ==
A rigorous and general proof can be found in [[John Larry Kelly, Jr|Kelly's]] original paper<ref name="original Kelly article" /> or in some of the other references listed below. Some corrections have been published.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Thorp |first=E. O. |author-link=Edward O. Thorp |date=1969 |title=Optimal Gambling Systems for Favorable Games |url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bsmsp/1200512159 |journal=Revue de l'Institut International de Statistique / Review of the International Statistical Institute |publisher=International Statistical Institute (ISI) |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=273–293 |doi=10.2307/1402118 |jstor=1402118 |mr=0135630|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
We give the following non-rigorous argument for the case with <math>g = l = 1</math> (a 50:50 "even money" bet) to show the general idea and provide some insights.<ref name="original Kelly article" />
When <math>g = l = 1</math>, a Kelly bettor bets <math>2p - 1</math> times their initial wealth <math>W</math>, as shown above. If they win, they have <math>2pW</math> after one bet. If they lose, they have <math>2(1 - p)W</math>. Suppose they make <math>N</math> bets like this, and win <math>K</math> times out of this series of <math>N</math> bets. The resulting wealth will be:
<math display="block">2^Np^K(1-p)^{N-K}W \! .</math>
The ordering of the wins and losses does not affect the resulting wealth. Suppose another bettor bets a different amount, <math>(2p - 1 + \Delta)W</math> for some value of <math>\Delta</math> (where <math>\Delta</math> may be positive or negative). They will have <math>(2p + \Delta)W</math> after a win and <math>[2(1-p)-\Delta]W</math> after a loss. After the same series of wins and losses as the Kelly bettor, they will have:
<math display="block">(2p+\Delta)^K[2(1-p)-\Delta]^{N-K}W</math>
Take the derivative of this with respect to <math>\Delta</math> and get:
<math display="block">K(2p+\Delta)^{K-1}[2(1-p)-\Delta]^{N-K}W-(N-K)(2p+\Delta)^K[2(1-p)-\Delta]^{N-K-1}W</math>
The function is maximized when this derivative is equal to zero, which occurs at:
<math display="block">K[2(1-p)-\Delta]=(N-K)(2p+\Delta)</math>
which implies that
<math display="block">\Delta=2\left(\frac{K}{N}-p\right)</math>
but the proportion of winning bets will [[ergodicity|eventually converge]] to:
<math display="block">\lim_{N \to +\infty}\frac{K}{N}=p</math>
according to the [[weak law of large numbers]].
So in the long run, final wealth is maximized by setting <math>\Delta</math> to zero, which means following the Kelly strategy.
This illustrates that Kelly has both a deterministic and a stochastic component. If one knows K and N and wishes to pick a constant fraction of wealth to bet each time (otherwise one could cheat and, for example, bet zero after the K<sup>th</sup> win knowing that the rest of the bets will lose), one will end up with the most money if one bets:
<math display="block">\left(2\frac{K}{N}-1\right)W</math>
each time. This is true whether <math>N</math> is small or large. The "long run" part of Kelly is necessary because K is not known in advance, just that as <math>N</math> gets large, <math>K</math> will approach <math>pN</math>. Someone who bets more than Kelly can do better if <math>K > pN</math> for a stretch; someone who bets less than Kelly can do better if <math>K<pN</math> for a stretch, but in the long run, Kelly always wins.
The heuristic proof for the general case proceeds as follows.{{Citation needed|date=April 2012}}
In a single trial, if one invests the fraction <math>f</math> of their capital, if the strategy succeeds, the capital at the end of the trial increases by the factor <math>1-f + f(1+g) = 1+fg</math>, and, likewise, if the strategy fails, the capital is decreased by the factor <math>1-fl</math>. Thus at the end of <math>N</math> trials (with <math>pN</math> successes and <math>qN</math> failures), the starting capital of $1 yields
<math display="block">C_N=(1+fg)^{pN}(1-fl)^{qN}.</math>
Maximizing <math>\log(C_N)/N</math>, and consequently <math>C_N</math>, with respect to <math>f</math> leads to the desired result
<math display="block">f^{*}=p/l-q/g .</math>
[[Edward O. Thorp]] provided a more detailed discussion of this formula for the general case.<ref name="edwardothorp.com" /> There, it can be seen that the substitution of <math>p</math> for the ratio of the number of "successes" to the number of trials implies that the number of trials must be very large, since <math>p</math> is defined as the limit of this ratio as the number of trials goes to infinity. In brief, betting <math>f</math> each time will likely maximize the wealth growth rate only in the case where the number of trials is very large, and <math>p</math>, <math>g</math>, and <math>l</math> are the same for each trial. In practice, this is a matter of playing the same game over and over, where the probability of winning and the payoff odds are always the same.  In the heuristic proof above, <math>pN</math> successes and <math>qN</math> failures are highly likely only for very large <math>N</math>.

=== Multiple outcomes ===
Kelly's criterion may be generalized<ref name="many horses">{{Cite journal |last1=Smoczynski |first1=Peter |last2=Tomkins |first2=Dave |date=2010 |title=An explicit solution to the problem of optimizing the allocations of a bettor's wealth when wagering on horse races |url=https://drive.google.com/file/d/1aLBmzUMUNIzRs9pNsU5e0acrzGdt4AGU/view |journal=Mathematical Scientist |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=10–17}}</ref> on gambling on many mutually exclusive outcomes, such as in horse races. Suppose there are several mutually exclusive outcomes. The probability that the <math>k</math>-th horse wins the race is <math>p_k</math>, the total amount of bets placed on <math>k</math>-th horse is <math>B_k</math>, and
<math display="block">\beta_k=\frac{B_k}{\sum_i B_i}=\frac{D}{1+Q_k} ,</math>
where <math>Q_k</math> are the pay-off odds. <math>D=1-tt</math>, is the dividend rate where <math>tt</math> is the track take or tax, <math>\frac{D}{\beta_k}</math> is the revenue rate after deduction of the track take when <math>k</math>-th horse wins. The fraction of the bettor's funds to bet on <math>k</math>-th horse is <math>f_k</math>. Kelly's criterion for gambling with multiple mutually exclusive outcomes gives an algorithm for finding the optimal set <math>S^o</math> of outcomes on which it is reasonable to bet and it gives explicit formula for finding the optimal fractions <math>f^o_k</math> of bettor's wealth to be bet on the outcomes included in the optimal set <math>S^o</math>.
The algorithm for the optimal set of outcomes consists of four steps:<ref name="many horses" />
# Calculate the expected revenue rate for all possible (or only for several of the most promising) outcomes: <math display="block">er_i = \frac{Dp_i}{\beta_i} = p_i(Q_i + 1)</math>
# Reorder the outcomes so that the new sequence <math>er_k</math> is non-increasing.  Thus <math>er_1</math> will be the best bet.
# Set <math>S = \varnothing</math> (the [[empty set]]), <math>k = 1</math>, <math>R(S)=1</math>.  Thus the best bet <math>er_k = er_1</math> will be considered first.
# Repeat:
#:If <math>er_k=\frac{D}{\beta_k}p_k > R(S)</math> then insert <math>k</math>-th outcome into the set: <math>S = S \cup \{k\}</math>, recalculate <math>R(S)</math> according to the formula: <math display="block">R(S) = \frac{D\sum_{k \notin S}p_k}{D-\sum_{k \in S}\beta_k}</math>  and then set <math>k = k+1</math>, {{pb}} Otherwise, set <math>S^o=S</math> and stop the repetition.

If the optimal set <math>S^o</math> is empty then do not bet at all. If the set <math>S^o</math> of optimal outcomes is not empty, then the optimal fraction <math>f^o_k</math> to bet on <math>k</math>-th outcome may be calculated from this formula:
<math display="block">f_i = p_i - \beta_i \frac{\sum_{k \notin S}p_k}{\left(D - \sum_{k \in S}\beta_k\right)}.</math>

One may prove<ref name="many horses" /> that
<math display="block">R(S^o)=1-\sum_{i \in S^o}{f^o_i}</math>
where the right hand-side is the reserve rate{{clarify|reason=not mentioned before|date=June 2012}}. Therefore, the requirement <math>er_k=\frac{D}{\beta_k}p_k > R(S)</math> may be interpreted<ref name="many horses" /> as follows: <math>k</math>-th outcome is included in the set <math>S^o</math> of optimal outcomes if and only if its expected revenue rate is greater than the reserve rate. The formula for the optimal fraction <math>f^o_k</math> may be interpreted as the excess of the expected revenue rate of <math>k</math>-th horse over the reserve rate divided by the revenue after deduction of the track take when <math>k</math>-th horse wins or as the excess of the probability of <math>k</math>-th horse winning over the reserve rate divided by revenue after deduction of the track take when <math>k</math>-th horse wins. The binary growth exponent is

<math display="block">G^o=\sum_{i \in S}{p_i\log_2(er_i)} + \left(1-\sum_{i \in S}{p_i}\right)\log_2(R(S^o)) ,</math>
and the [[doubling time]] is
<math display="block">T_d=\frac{1}{G^o}.</math>

This method of selection of optimal bets may be applied also when probabilities <math>p_k</math> are known only for several most promising outcomes, while the remaining outcomes have no chance to win. In this case it must be that
<math display="block">\sum_i{p_i} < 1 ,</math> and
<math display="block">\sum_i{\beta_i} < 1</math>.

=== Stock investments ===
The second-order [[Taylor series|Taylor polynomial]] can be used as a good approximation of the main criterion. Primarily, it is useful for stock investment, where the fraction devoted to investment is based on simple characteristics that can be estimated from existing historical data – [[expected value]] and [[variance]]. This approximation may offer similar results as the original criterion,<ref>{{Cite conference |last1=Marek |first1=Patrice |last2=Ťoupal |first2=Tomáš |last3=Vávra |first3=František |date=2016 |title=Efficient Distribution of Investment Capital |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/308919565 |conference=34th International Conference Mathematical Methods in Economics |pages=540–545 |id=MME2016 }}</ref> but in some cases the solution obtained may be infeasible.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Hsieh |first1=Chung-Han |last2=Barmish |first2=B. Ross |author-link2=B. Ross Barmish |date=2015 |title=On Kelly betting: some limitations |conference=53rd Annual Allerton Conference on Communication, Control, and Computing |location=Monticello, Illinois |publisher=IEEE |pages=165–172 }}</ref>

For single assets (stock, [[index fund]], etc.), and a risk-free rate, it is straightforward to obtain the optimal fraction to invest through [[geometric Brownian motion]].
The [[stochastic differential equation]] governing the evolution of a lognormally distributed asset <math>S</math> at time <math>t</math> (<math>S_t</math>) is

<math display="block">dS_t/S_t=\mu dt+\sigma dW_t</math>

whose solution is

<math display="block">S_t = S_0\exp\left( \left(\mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \right)t + \sigma W_t\right)</math>

where <math>W_t</math> is a [[Wiener process]], and <math>\mu</math> (percentage drift) and <math>\sigma</math> (the percentage volatility) are constants. Taking expectations of the logarithm:
<math display="block">\mathbb{E} \log(S_t)=\log(S_0)+\left(\mu- \frac {\sigma^2}{2}\right)t.</math>
Then the expected log return <math>R_s</math> is
<math display="block">R_s = \left(\mu -\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\,\right).</math>
Consider a portfolio made of an asset <math>S</math> and a bond paying risk-free rate <math>r</math>, with fraction <math>f</math> invested in <math>S</math> and <math>(1-f)</math> in the bond. The aforementioned equation for <math>dS_t</math> must be modified by this fraction, i.e. <math>\frac{dS_t'}{S_t'} =f\frac{dS_t}{S_t}</math>, with associated solution

<math display="block">S'_t = S'_0\exp\left( \left(f\mu - \frac{(f\sigma)^2}{2} \right)t + f\sigma W_t\right)</math>

the expected one-period return is given by

<math display="block">\mathbb{E}{\left(\left[\frac{S'_1}{S'_0} - 1\right] + ( 1 - f)r \right)} = \mathbb{E}{\left( \left[\exp\left( \left(f\mu - \frac{(f\sigma)^2}{2} \right) + f\sigma W_1\right) - 1 \right]\right)} + (1 - f) r</math>

For small <math>\mu</math>, <math>\sigma</math>, and <math>W_t</math>, the solution can be expanded to first order to yield an approximate increase in wealth

<math display="block">G(f) = f\mu - \frac {(f\sigma)^2}{2} + (1-f)\ r.</math>

Solving <math>\max (G(f))</math> we obtain
<math display="block">f^* = \frac {\mu - r} {\sigma^2}.</math>
<math>f^*</math> is the fraction that maximizes the expected logarithmic return, and so, is the Kelly fraction.
Thorp<ref name="edwardothorp.com" /> arrived at the same result but through a different derivation.
Remember that <math>\mu</math> is different from the asset log return <math>R_s</math>. Confusing this is a common mistake made by websites and articles talking about the Kelly Criterion.

For multiple assets, consider a market with <math>n</math> correlated stocks <math>S_k</math> with stochastic returns <math>r_k</math>, <math>k= 1, \dots, n,</math> and a riskless bond with return <math>r</math>. An investor puts a fraction <math>u_k</math> of their capital in <math>S_k</math> and the rest is invested in the bond. [[Without loss of generality]], assume that investor's starting capital is equal to 1.
According to the Kelly criterion one should maximize
<math display="block">\mathbb{E}\left[ \ln\left((1 + r) + \sum\limits_{k=1}^n  u_k(r_k -r) \right) \right].</math>
Expanding this with a [[Taylor series]] around <math>\vec{u_0} = (0, \ldots , 0)</math> we obtain
<math display="block">\mathbb{E} \left[ \ln(1+r) + \sum\limits_{k=1}^{n} \frac{u_k(r_k - r)}{1+r} -
\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n} u_k u_j \frac{(r_k
-r)(r_j - r)}{(1+r)^2} \right].</math>
Thus we reduce the optimization problem to [[quadratic programming]] and the unconstrained solution
is
<math display="block">
\vec{u^{\star}} = (1+r) (  \widehat{\Sigma} )^{-1} ( \widehat{\vec{r}} - r )
</math>
where <math>\widehat{\vec{r}}</math> and <math>\widehat{\Sigma}</math> are the vector of means and the matrix of second mixed noncentral moments of the excess returns.
There is also a numerical algorithm for the fractional Kelly strategies and for the optimal solution under no leverage and no short selling constraints.<ref>{{Cite SSRN |last=Nekrasov |first=Vasily |date=2013 |title=Kelly Criterion for Multivariate Portfolios: A Model-Free Approach |ssrn=2259133 }}</ref>

== Bernoulli ==
In a 1738 article, [[Daniel Bernoulli]] suggested that, when one has a choice of bets or investments, one should choose that with the highest [[geometric mean]] of outcomes. This is mathematically equivalent to the Kelly criterion, although the motivation is different (Bernoulli wanted to resolve the [[St. Petersburg paradox]]).

An English translation of the Bernoulli article was not published until 1954,<ref name="Bernoulli translation">{{Cite journal |last=Bernoulli |first=Daniel |author-link=Daniel Bernoulli |date=1954 |title=Exposition of a New Theory on the Measurement of Risk |journal=[[Econometrica]] |publisher=[[The Econometric Society]] |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=22–36 |doi=10.2307/1909829 |jstor=1909829|s2cid=9165746 |url=https://psych.fullerton.edu/mbirnbaum/psych466/articles/bernoulli_econometrica.pdf}} English translation of 1738 paper.</ref> but the work was well known among mathematicians and economists.

== Criticism ==
Although the Kelly strategy's promise of doing better than any other strategy in the long run seems compelling, some economists have argued strenuously against it, mainly because an individual's specific investing constraints may override the desire for optimal growth rate.<ref name="Poundstone book article" /> One such economist is [[Paul Samuelson]], who stated that a flaw of the Kelly Criterion was risk tolerance. He stated that, while maximizing log growth results in large growth rates, it is not worth the losses from a wrong bet. This preference for lower risk is a critique of maximizing log growth and the Kelly Criterion, as the negative utility of losses would be too much to bear for those individuals.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Paul |first1=Samuelson |title=Why we should not make mean log of wealth big though years to act are long |url=http://www-stat.wharton.upenn.edu/~steele/Courses/434/434Context/Kelly%20Resources/Samuelson1979.pdf |publisher=North Holland Publishing Company |access-date=21 August 2026 |quote=When you lose - and you sure can lose - with N large, you can lose real big.}}</ref>

The conventional alternative is [[expected utility]] theory which says bets should be sized to [[Optimization (mathematics)|maximize]] the [[Expected value|expected]] utility of the outcome (to an individual with [[logarithm]]ic utility, the Kelly bet maximizes expected utility, so there is no conflict; moreover, Kelly's original paper clearly states the need for a utility function in the case of gambling games which are played finitely many times<ref name="original Kelly article" />). Even Kelly supporters usually argue for fractional Kelly (betting a fixed fraction {{mvar|k}} of the amount recommended by Kelly, which is more rigorously calculated with the utility function {{tmath|1=u(x) = \tfrac{x^{1-1/k} }{1-1/k} }} when {{math|''k'' ≠ 1}}) for a variety of practical reasons, such as wishing to reduce volatility, or protecting against non-deterministic errors in their advantage (edge) calculations.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Thorp |first=E.O. |date=May 2008 |title=The Kelly Criterion: Part I |work=[[Wilmott (magazine)|Wilmott]] |page= }}</ref>{{Page needed|date=March 2026}} In colloquial terms, the Kelly criterion requires accurate probability values, which isn't always possible for real-world event outcomes. When a gambler overestimates their true probability of winning, the criterion value calculated will diverge from the optimal, increasing the risk of ruin.

In the stock market, the Kelly bet can be thought as ''time diversification'', which is taking equal risk during different sequential time periods (as opposed to taking equal risk in different assets for asset diversification). There is a difference between time diversification and asset diversification, which was raised by [[Paul A. Samuelson]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Samuelson |first=Paul A. |date=April 1963 |title=Risk and uncertainty: a fallacy of large numbers |work=Scientia |issue=6 |volume=57 |pages=153–158 }}</ref> There is also a difference between ensemble-averaging (utility calculation) and time-averaging (Kelly multi-period betting over a single time path in real life). The debate was renewed by evoking [[ergodicity]] breaking.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Peters |first1=Ole |last2=Gell-Mann |first2=Murray |title=Evaluating gambles using dynamics |journal=Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science |date=2015 |volume=26 |issue=2 |page=023103 |doi=10.1063/1.4940236|pmid=26931584 |s2cid=9726238 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1405.0585 }}</ref> Yet the difference between [[ergodicity]] breaking and [[Knightian uncertainty]] should be recognized.<ref>{{cite SSRN |last1=Ford |first1=Matthew |last2=Kay |first2=John |date=2022 |title=Psychology is Fundamental: The Limitations of Growth-Optimal Approaches to Decision Making under Uncertainty |ssrn=4140625 <!--|doi=10.2139/ssrn.4140625 |s2cid=250132554 |doi-access=free -->}}</ref>
